cards.title: Designing a RAG system end to end
questions: walk me through how you would design a rag system end to end
design a retrieval augmented generation pipeline from ingestion to answer
rag system design question
how would you build question answering over internal documents

cards.answer: I design it as a funnel where every stage can be checked on its own. Ingest with a stable ID per document, so any answer traces back to its source; in the archive search the Box file_id rides through all eight stages. Chunk to the size the model handles well, which I measure rather than assume. Embed with one model, L2-normalize, and pick the FAISS index for the scale. Retrieve with a calibrated threshold plus structured filters, so the LLM only sees a few dozen candidates. For citations I don't let the model quote. In Evidence Desk the model returns block IDs and the label, and code copies the exact text and checks its hash, which removed every copy failure. I measure retrieval coverage separately, because when the right block never arrives, no prompt can fix it.

cards.answer: I use hybrid retrieval whenever exact signals exist, because vectors are good at meaning and weak on identifiers. In procurement the exact tier, a dictionary keyed on manufacturer and part number, answers in under 2ms and always runs; FAISS covers only what it misses, since semantic matches alone carry too many false positives for numbers people will act on. In the HERDS classifier I blend a semantic score with a keyword-overlap score at 0.75 to 0.25, which beat either signal alone on the validation set, with a 0.12 floor before any label is assigned. The legislative platform pairs MiniLM and FAISS search with structured filters and keyword matching on raw extracted text. I haven't run BM25 itself in production; I'd tune its weight the same way, on labeled queries.

cards.answer: I pick the index for the scale and the recall I need. For the legacy archive, thousands of summaries, I used IndexFlatIP over L2-normalized MiniLM embeddings, so inner product equals cosine and search is exact; the HNSW version persists to disk and loads instantly with no database server. At 5.19 million product vectors, about an 8GB index, exhaustive search stops making sense, so procurement uses IVFFlat with 4,096 lists and nprobe 64, returning candidates in 75 to 110ms. nprobe is the recall dial: probe more lists for better recall and slower queries. I build indexes offline once and rebuild only when descriptions change, not prices. And I keep vectors out of the main table: at five million rows, 384-dimension embeddings are roughly 7.5 GB that almost nothing reads.

questions: how do you serve llms efficiently

inference server tuning

cards.answer: Most throughput problems I've seen live in the serving layer. On our L4, Ollama handled one request at a time: throughput stayed flat at about 9 images a minute from concurrency 1 to 8 while p50 latency rose 8.18x and the GPU sat at 28 to 31%. vLLM's continuous batching took the same card to 55.4 images a minute at concurrency 8 and 96 to 97% utilization. The KV cache is the next limit. Mistral with 3,000-token chunks saw p99 grow from 15s to 74s between concurrency 1 and 24, head-of-line blocking from cache pressure, so it was dropped. I choose the operating point by sweeping concurrency: for Llama 3.1 8B, quality held within 0.6 points from 1 to 24, so 12 to 24 became purely a throughput and latency call.

cards.title: Fitting a model on a GPU: quantization and VRAM budgeting
questions: how do you fit a model on a gpu

cards.answer: I budget VRAM as weights plus KV cache plus runtime overhead, then check the real allocation. AWQ is how a 7 to 8B model fits our 22.5 GB L4 with room to batch: about 4 GB at idle, leaving roughly 18 GB for KV cache and co-resident pipelines. On my personal RTX 5090 I serve AWQ and FP8 models through vLLM, Qwen3 32B AWQ among them, and I sized a context change from 4,096 to 16,384 tokens with KV-cache arithmetic and a benchmark before adopting it. Two lessons came from failures. Ollama's keep_alive held about 6 GB and blocked vLLM's cache allocation, and right-sizing one model's allocation freed about 15 GB so the archival pipeline could share the server. The format matters too: the same 32B model accepted 3 groups on vLLM with AWQ and 1 on Ollama with Q4_K_M.

cards.answer: I write the SLO down before the run and project it against the real corpus, not the test sample. For the legislative pipeline the 50-state target was about 75,000 bills a week in an 18-hour processing window: 1.157 bills a second sustained, 2.41 at peak. Llama 3.1 8B on one L4 measured 0.88 chunks a second at concurrency 24; at 2.40 chunks per bill on the real length distribution, that's 0.367 bills a second. That passes the Illinois workload with 2.05x headroom and misses the national target by 3.16x, so the hardware ask became specific: about three L4s or one A100-class card for steady state, about seven L4s or H100-class hardware for bursts. I track p99 as well as the mean, because the tail is what blocks a batch queue.

cards.answer: I treat a prompt like code with a version, because a silent prompt edit invalidates every comparison after it. In Skyrule, my personal project, the generation prompt gets a new immutable id on every change, and in the document evaluation any new prompt or variant became a new protocol version with its own frozen cases. The extraction schemas I design carry model-version and prompt-version columns, so every stored value says what produced it. On the craft side, I bundle related questions in one prompt so earlier answers give context to later ones, state rejection rules explicitly, and ask for output only, with no preamble. When a validator rejected acceptable text in a Skyrule pilot, fixing the prompt and the check together raised plan acceptance from 6 of 31 to 14 of 31.

cards.answer: I build the evaluation so the numbers can't drift between runs. Cases are frozen and hashed before any model sees them; every request, client setting and scorer is fingerprinted, and the merge tool refuses rows that fail the check. That's how two machines, two coding assistants and weeks of runs produced 40,975 scored rows in one report. Scoring is code against answer keys wherever a key exists: character error, TEDS, relaxed accuracy, numeric recall. Failures and truncations stay in the denominator as zero. I use a model as grader only where judgment can't be computed, and I check it first: two independent Opus passes agreed on 60 of 60 cells, and Skyrule's grader must clear 85% agreement at the Wilson lower bound. Regression means rerunning the same frozen suite and comparing cell by cell.

cards.answer: I design agents around what they may not do. In my personal projects each Claude Code agent has a written charter and a scope generated from a machine-readable ownership map, and pre-execution hooks refuse any file write or shell command outside it, so staying in its lane is enforced, not requested. Memory is files with rules a model won't hold on its own: each memory names a source file whose hash is stored, near-duplicates are refused, and an append-only decision log is searched before anyone asks me a question. Work runs through one job queue with lanes, dependencies, three attempts by default and finish checks that decide done by evidence rather than exit code. A weekly usage budget caps launches, and nothing is pushed or published without my explicit go.

cards.answer: In Skyrule, my personal project, agents don't talk to each other in real time; they coordinate through owned files, queue dependencies and dated handoff documents, so every exchange leaves a record a new session can read. The failures I've hit were mostly coordination and control problems. On Windows, a hook that blocked by exit code only produced a warning, so the guard now denies through an explicit decision. A usage-limit detector matched an agent's own report and paused a lane for a day. A job launched from a chat session died with its console, so jobs now launch only from the scheduled task. A shared status log got a single locking writer, tested with four writers at once. Shell writes are still guarded by heuristics, so an ownership audit runs before every merge.

questions: how would you design a multimodal document pipeline

cards.answer: I split a document into extraction types and route each to what measured best, because no single model wins. In my October evaluation, Qwen3-VL 8B on a 12 GB laptop read prose crops at about 1.2% character error, matching the 32B models. On fresh financial tables the small PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 parser beat Qwen3-VL 32B, 0.852 against 0.762 TEDS. For charts the method mattered as much as the model: self-check lifted one model 26.5 points and sank another 43.5. DocLayout-YOLO finds tables and figures, but masking them before page OCR raised word F1 while cutting numeric recall from 0.872 to 0.694, so it stays experimental. For archive photographs I used LLaVA descriptions instead of Tesseract, since the archive held photographs, not just scanned text.

cards.answer: My rule is to do everything deterministic before any model runs, then send each task to the cheapest model that clears its bar. Procurement is the clearest example: an exact dictionary lookup on manufacturer and part number answers in under 2ms, FAISS narrows six million rows to a median of 44 candidates in 75 to 110ms, and only then does a 7B model judge equivalence, in 5 to 8 seconds. If the LLM is offline, the exact tier still returns. The archival build follows the same order: free filters first, and no file reaches enrichment unless triage selected it. In Skyrule, my personal project, routing comes from measurement on my own GPU: Claude models for design, review and audit, local Qwen models for bulk generation and grading, small models for utilities.

cards.answer: I cache at three levels: model responses, expensive artifacts and computed results. Procurement caches LLM responses by prompt hash, so a repeated query costs nothing. Indexes and embeddings are built offline once: FAISS indexes live as files on disk, the research pipeline caches its taxonomy embeddings and vocabulary, and browse categories are pre-indexed at API startup in about 30 seconds so browsing is instant. On the legislative platform, live impact scoring is cache-first: each bill and prompt pair is scored once and read instantly after, and nightly rescoring uses content hashes so only changed bills are re-evaluated. Streamlit data loads sit behind st.cache_data with a one-hour TTL, so the 4 AM rescore shows up the same day. Every cache has an explicit invalidation key: prompt hash, content hash or TTL.

cards.title: Retries, idempotent writes and rollback
questions: retries and timeouts in ai pipelines
idempotent writes
how do you make a rerun safe

poison pill records
retry ceiling
how does she handle retries

cards.answer: I design every write so a rerun is harmless and every failure is bounded. The research proposals pipeline inserts with WHERE NOT EXISTS or MERGE, checks the row count it wrote against what it attempted and raises if they differ, and prints the exact rollback SQL on every run. Long jobs checkpoint and resume rather than restart: the legislative extractor flushes in batches and can be killed without double-writing. Retries need a ceiling. One malformed bill truncated, failed to parse, was never written, reappeared as new and failed again for six days; the fix was a length guard plus a retry limit that parks the record instead of reprocessing it forever. My job queue gives three attempts by default and flags runs that exceed a time limit set per lane.

cards.answer: I monitor for absence as much as for errors, because AI pipelines usually fail quietly. Every pipeline writes the same Parquet log schema, with PIPELINE_START and PIPELINE_END sentinel rows sharing a run ID; a start with no end, or no successful run inside the window, raises a silent-pipeline alert. Root failures are separated from the cascade they cause, and only critical ones send email, so alerts stay readable. Then I audit the monitor itself. On the legislative pipeline a stage reported success while producing zero output, so completion now requires a non-zero count, and alert delivery turned out never to be verified. Quarterly jobs get their own silence threshold, 2,400 hours with matching Grafana panels, instead of alerting for 89 days straight.

cards.answer: I start from a threat model and keep data where it belongs. In Skyrule, my personal project, a security function can block any merge or release that weakens a control. Its first pass produced the threat model, an IP-protection plan that keeps valuable logic server-side behind per-account rate limits, and scans with Bandit, Semgrep, pip-audit and a history-wide secret scan, which found no credentials. I locked down the internal API on a reviewed branch: authentication on every route, no prompt exposure, closed CORS and rate limits. I haven't built a dedicated prompt-injection filter; my control is privilege, since no agent can push or publish and write scope is enforced by hooks. At work, secrets sit in platform configuration with rotation through secondary keys, and training code was scrubbed of an embedded key before external review.

cards.answer: I test the deterministic code around the model as strictly as any software, and I test the checks themselves. In Skyrule, my personal project, each validator check is tested three ways: it must catch the defects I named (8 of 8 in v7), its false-alarm rate on previously accepted claims is reported, and mutation testing caught 21 of 21 deliberate breaks. CI proves 14 protected tests actually ran, because a silently skipped test leaves the build green. For the archival manifest I committed a 50-row synthetic fixture covering every format and status, plus a deliberately broken copy that trips each rule, so the suite runs with no data or credentials. My evaluation scorers are checked on golden inputs, and accessibility fixes were verified in a headless browser on the production Streamlit build.

cards.answer: I deploy through whatever the environment allows and fix what breaks on the way. The legislative app ships to Azure App Service through Local Git and the Oryx build. I resolved a .deployment file that blocked Oryx, SCM basic auth and dynamic port binding, and fixed an outage where the startup command reinstalled dependencies on every boot and killed the container with exit code 127. The university tenant blocks standard zip deploys, so Azure Functions deploy through Cloud Shell with a remote build. Scheduled work runs on cron and the JupyterHub Scheduler, payroll processing runs on GitHub Actions, and Actions workflows maintain the RIMS project board. After a function deploy I restart, wait for warm-up, then trigger, because stale workers can serve old code and look like a regression.

cards.answer: I design the API around tiers that can fail independently. The procurement FastAPI service has 10 endpoints: /health, /candidates for retrieval alone with no LLM, /compare for the full three-tier pipeline, browse and autocomplete routes pre-indexed at startup, and /trends over a precomputed savings table. If the LLM is down, exact matches and semantic candidates still return, so the service never returns nothing, and every result downloads as CSV for independent checking. The legislative Streamlit app uses st.navigation with app.py as a thin router, content in a pages folder, one auth gate and a shared accessible theme, plus pyarrow column pruning and cached loads for the Basic tier. Generation and display deploy separately, so a failed deep dive can't take down nightly scoring.

cards.answer: I write the contract before the code, enforce it in code and give every column an owner. The RIMS archival manifest is 116 columns, one row per file path, and each stage owns the columns it writes, so stages can be rerun or replaced independently. Keys are deterministic: file_uid is a blake2b hash of source and normalized path, so a re-crawl joins cleanly. Status columns stay null until a stage runs, which makes the work queue a query and separates not processed from processed and found nothing. The schema is validated against a synthetic fixture and a deliberately broken twin. The retirement rebuild froze its output contract at 4 files, 21 sheets and 436 columns, checked on every run, and every pipeline shares one Parquet logging schema.

cards.answer: I look at the shape of the work first, then push it into vectorized or precomputed form. Labeling 1.39 million legislative action rows one at a time wasn't runnable in the nightly window, so pass one applies combined regex with str.contains across the whole column, resolving 85 to 90% of rows in under 30 seconds, and rapidfuzz runs only on the remainder. In procurement, building a dictionary with itertuples takes about 90 seconds at startup and replaces a 1,700ms DataFrame scan per query with a lookup under 2ms. On Azure's Basic tier, pyarrow column pruning and cached loads kept the app within the tier's limits. Sharing one sentence encoder instead of loading two saved about 500MB and 30 seconds of startup. And adding about a hundred columns one at a time fragments a DataFrame, harmless at five rows and severe at five million.

cards.answer: I choose an embedding model for the domain vocabulary and the scale, then keep one semantic space per index. The archive search uses all-MiniLM-L6-v2 both to pick representative sentences before summarization and to index the summaries, so selection and search agree. Procurement uses bge-small-en-v1.5 at 384 dimensions over 5.19 million rows, with a cosine threshold of 0.85 that leaves a median of 44 candidates. The procurement index is built offline and reused; it needs rebuilding only when product descriptions change significantly, not when prices change. I also embed LLM summaries rather than raw text where text is noisy: summaries are clean and consistently phrased, which improved recall.

What I have done is size for scale from measurements. cards.answer: I work branch per issue with a pull request to main, even for notebooks, so review happens before work lands. On the RIMS archival build I set that convention for an engineer on her first project, with issues that carry an owner, dependencies and explicit done-when criteria, a Blocked column that names a person and a date, and type:decision labels holding the reasoning. In review I check behavior as well as the diff: for 29 pull requests from a cloud coding agent on Skyrule, my personal project, I fetched each into an isolated archive, ran the full suite and the regression checks, and verified ancestry before reporting a merge. I clean history before it goes public: one notebook carried 377 MB of embedded outputs, including email content, which I stripped first.

cards.title: PII in an LLM pipeline: two-layer anonymization
questions: how do you handle pii in an llm pipeline

cards.answer: I anonymize in two layers so the LLM never has to be the privacy control. In the email archive, Microsoft Presidio first detects structured PII such as names, phone numbers, emails and SSNs, and replaces it with typed placeholders like <PERSON1>, keeping the mapping separately. Then a local Llama 3.2 model writes a summary, instructed to generalize any remaining personal detail. Placeholder text produced more coherent summaries than raw text with names still in it. The model runs locally through Ollama. The failure to watch for is over-redaction: in the RIMS build the redaction layer labeled ZIP+4 codes as social security numbers and chart axis labels as card numbers, which would have stripped research data from the reading-room copy. So I check what gets removed, not only what survives.

cards.title: System design: extracting data from scanned PDFs with tables
questions: design a document extraction service for scanned pdfs

cards.answer: I'd build it as a queue of pages routed by content type, with evidence attached to every field. Intake identifies each file and page, and a native spreadsheet is parsed directly when the original exists. Scanned pages go through layout detection, then tables to a table model, prose to OCR and charts to a chart route, one model resident on the GPU at a time, with checkpoints and bounded retries. From my evaluation I'd start tables on PaddleOCR-VL-1.6, at 0.852 TEDS and 97.4% numeric recall on fresh financial tables. Fields come out by evidence ID, so code copies and hash-checks the source text, and unread pages are flagged, never skipped. Numbers get their own gate, since no model reached my 99% bar, so it ships review-assisted: a reviewer sees each value beside its page.

cards.answer: I've built close to this: price comparison over 6,068,888 catalog rows from four distributors. First fix the data. A pack-size field covering 99.9% of rows turned prices into unit prices and removed 49.1% of the apparent savings. Then an exact tier, a dictionary on manufacturer and part number, answering in under 2ms. Then embeddings: bge-small-en-v1.5 into a FAISS IVFFlat index of 5.19 million vectors, nprobe 64, with a cosine floor of 0.85, returning a median of 44 candidates in 75 to 110ms. A 7B model judges equivalence only on those candidates and returns JSON, and prices are compared in code. Offline index builds, response caching and a 30-query eval set round it out.

cards.answer: I start by asking whether the inputs, the infrastructure or the model changed, and I check output volume and shape before trusting a green status. Three real cases. An extraction stage failed silently for 11 nights; the cause was a kernel update that disabled the GPU driver, and I protected the catch-up so no data was skipped. A six-day repeating alarm traced to one malformed bill retried forever. And nightly scoring formatted inputs differently from training, fixed with a shared input module verified byte-identical on 36,028 inputs. Aggregate metrics can hide individual faults, too: a high AUC concealed a probability trail where stalled bills kept their peak score, which surfaced only once users could see the trail.

cards.answer: I choose by data sensitivity, volume and latency. Ollama is simple to run and fine for one request at a time, but on our L4 it serialized requests. vLLM is what I use for volume, because continuous batching took the same card from about 9 to 55.4 images a minute; on an air-gapped server I staged the weights by hand to get it. Hosted APIs fit low-latency, user-facing work on non-sensitive data. The legislative platform is deliberately hybrid: bulk extraction and scoring on on-prem vLLM at no marginal cost, gpt-4o-mini on Azure OpenAI for in-app briefings, GPT-4.1 behind the Copilot chatbot, and Groq's hosted Llama for briefings, degrading gracefully without a key. Sensitive archives stay on local models only.

cards.answer: I sample GPU utilization, VRAM and power in the same window as the workload, because averages from separate runs hide the signature I'm looking for. On the archival image job, one-second nvidia-smi sampling showed 28 to 31% utilization with VRAM and power flat while latency climbed, which meant the GPU was waiting on serialized requests; a faster card would have recovered nothing. After the move to vLLM the same card ran at 96 to 97%, 19 to 20 GB of VRAM and 71 to 72W, against about 27W before. I apply the USE method (utilization, saturation, errors) and preflight every run to confirm the GPU is idle first, at 3 MiB used. Longer sweeps also track temperature and KV cache against alarms; the L4 peaked at 70°C.

cards.answer: I use AI coding assistants heavily and give them explicit limits. For the document evaluation I set the rule that assistants write and orchestrate code only: local models and OCR engines do all the reading and judging, assistants see aggregate metrics, and no work document leaves approved storage. A privacy gate script in the repository denies institutional identifiers before anything is committed. In my personal projects, agents work inside hook-enforced scopes, a quality agent can block a release in writing, and every done claim needs re-runnable evidence. I review agent pull requests the way I'd review anyone's: isolated checkout, full test suite, regression checks. For judgment calls an independent second model reviews generated text only, never private inputs.

cards.answer: A good evaluation set looks like real traffic, includes the hard cases on purpose and is frozen before anyone tunes against it. The procurement set has 30 hand-curated queries covering exact matches, vague natural language, part-number lookups and edge cases like pack size, concentration mismatch and accessories, each with an expected tier, price range and minimum alternatives. Development and held-out sets stay separate: the document evaluation froze 2,181 held-out cases and used them once. Splits happen at the level that prevents leakage: the legislative model holds out a whole General Assembly session. And labels need a definition first: in the archival image pilot 58 of 79 flags were ambiguous, so the RIMS build requires a written appraisal policy and a 300 to 500 file hand-labeled gold set before triage work.

cards.answer: I write systems so the next engineer can change them without me in the room. Contracts live in code: a schema module with validation, fixtures that run with no data or credentials, an output contract checked on every run. Decisions are recorded with their reasons, in type:decision issues on the RIMS build and an append-only log in my personal projects. Code is single-responsibility service modules under thin controllers, SQL lives in versioned files instead of inside a tool, and config is parameterized with a committed .example template so secrets stay out. Each inherited proof of concept got a README saying what's reusable and what's known to be broken. On the legislative app I wrote an Accessibility Guide with patterns, scripts and a decision log for future contributors.

cards.answer: I moved to vLLM because the measurements said the server was the bottleneck: Ollama held throughput flat across concurrency with the L4 28 to 31% busy, so a bigger GPU would have bought nothing. The server is air-gapped, and curl -v showed the block was specific: GitHub, PyPI and the Ollama registry worked, HuggingFace died at the TLS handshake. That turned no internet into no HuggingFace, so I stage weights on a laptop, copy them over with scp and point vLLM at the local path. Three things broke in the 0.6.6 stand-up: mistral_common had moved an import, transformers was a major version ahead, and Ollama's keep_alive held about 6 GB that vLLM's KV cache needed. I fixed them in order and isolated vLLM in its own conda environment. Result: 6.22x throughput on the same card.

cards.answer: Each alternative failed a specific stage that Llama passed. On parse-OK, Llama 3.1 8B led at every chunk size, 85.0 to 92.5%, peaking at 1,200 tokens, while no Mistral or Qwen cell reached 73%. A blind rubric review on 60 cells confirmed the ranking. Qwen went out because its own parse-OK misranked its chunk sizes; its peak was valid JSON full of None. Mistral went out on the tail: with 3,000-token prompts its p99 grew from 15s to 74s by concurrency 24 under KV cache pressure. A 14B model given whole bills scored 45.0%. At 1,200 tokens the median bill of 1,051 tokens is one chunk, and quality held within 0.6 points from concurrency 1 to 24, so 12 to 24 is where the GPU is used well.

cards.answer: In Skyrule, my personal project, code lays out what two people's traits support, the local model plans a reading claim by claim, code validates every claim, then the model writes one sentence per approved claim and code checks again. I iterated the validator through seven versions from my own reviews, adding checks for truncated claims, causal leaps, wrong-person attribution and contradictions. Each new check must catch the defects I named (8 of 8 in v7), report its false-alarm rate on previously accepted claims, and survive mutation testing, 21 of 21 deliberate breaks caught. Checks can be too strict: an over-literal one rejected good text, and fixing it raised plan acceptance from 6 to 14 of 31. Canary 1 failed its check at 18 of 50, so five wording habits became new checks before any full run.

cards.title: What breaks first at 10x scale
questions: what would break first at 10x scale

cards.answer: GPU throughput breaks first, and I know by how much. The 50-state target is about seven times Illinois volume, and one L4 running Llama 3.1 8B at concurrency 24 falls 3.16x short of the steady-state SLO and 6.57x short of peak burst. Next is the length tail: 12% of bills exceed 10,000 tokens and the longest is over a million, so chunk counts per bill, and KV cache pressure if chunks grow, rise faster than bill counts. Uniform chunking is the next thing I'd change, with adaptive tiers by bill length. On the app side, memory already bit once: semantic search failed under memory pressure until the tier moved to Premium v3 and loads became selective. The data pipeline itself scales, because ingestion is hash-based and only changed sessions download.

cards.answer: I split by who is waiting and what it costs. On the legislative platform, heavy work runs as batch on institution-owned GPU: nightly feature extraction and impact scoring on vLLM, at no marginal cost, with nobody waiting. User-facing requests go to managed inference on Azure OpenAI, where latency matters. The two meet in one result schema. A user's prompt against a single bill can be scored live, stored and read instantly afterward, and the nightly batch writes the same long-format table, one row per user, prompt and bill, so either path can fill a cell. The split began as a workaround when the campus network blocked the server from the database, and became a deliberate design. Features are extracted once per bill, so adding a user never re-extracts the corpus.

cards.answer: I treat the token budget as part of the design, because truncation fails quietly. When Qwen 2.5 14B got whole 5,000-token bills, too little room was left to finish an 11-field JSON: 54% of outputs were partial, averaging 1.2 missing fields, with zero outright failures. In the document evaluation every task had a fixed budget, from 300 to 6,000 tokens, and a truncated answer scored zero instead of being rerun with more room. That rule exposed a thinking build that spent its budget on hidden reasoning, so it was removed. A hosted model first tested at a 600-token budget truncated; raising the budget alone changed nothing, while enabling reasoning did. For user-written profile context, I set explicit length limits and explained them to users.

cards.answer: I validate a cheap metric against a careful one before I tune on it. Parse-OK rate, the share of outputs that parse into every field, is fast and scales, so I tested it twice on the legislative sweep. Across models it held: a blind rubric review on 60 cells ranked the three models the same way, and two independent scoring passes agreed on all 60. Within a model it failed. In every informative pair the smaller chunk size scored at least as well on substance, even where parse-OK disagreed, because larger chunks produced confident answers about the wrong section of the bill. For Qwen, the parse-OK peak was valid JSON full of the string None. So parse-OK ranks models for me, and chunk sizes need substantive review.

iv-chunking: what is lost in the middle

iv-chunking.answer: I treat chunk size as a measured parameter, measured on the real length distribution. On the legislative pipeline every 7B-class model degraded past roughly 2,000 tokens, which let me choose chunk size separately from the model. The vLLM sweep then showed what parse rates hid: larger chunks caused off-section drift, where the model answers confidently about a neighboring section of the bill. Llama 3.1 8B at 1,200 tokens stayed on-chunk and reached 92.5% parse-OK, while a 14B model given whole 5,000-token bills scored 45.0%, so more context made things worse. I also check boundary artifacts: a dip at 4,000 tokens turned out to be thin tail chunks. When a document must be summarized whole, I compress it semantically first, keeping the 250 most representative sentences rather than truncating the head.

iv-structured-output.answer: I get reliable structured output by forcing a schema, counting parse status as its own quality signal and keeping code responsible for anything exact. Every chunk is marked OK, PARTIAL or EMPTY, so malformed output is counted rather than silently absorbed. On the archival images, one combined prompt returning JSON for all six fields was 1.61x faster than three calls and parsed 100% on five fields and 94% on the title. In the document evaluation, schema forcing, temperature 0 and fixed token budgets were fingerprinted for every model, and truncated answers scored zero instead of being retried. Two lessons stuck. Valid JSON isn't a correct answer: one model returned every field as the string None. And when an answer must quote a source, the model returns block IDs and code copies the text.

iv-hallucination.answer: My main defense is architectural: the model proposes, code verifies, and anything that must be exact never comes from generation. In procurement the LLM only judges product equivalence on about 50 pre-filtered candidates, and savings are computed in code from its JSON. In my document evaluation the model returns evidence block IDs, and code copies the text and checks its hash, which removed every quote-copy failure. In Skyrule, my personal project, a local model plans a reading claim by claim, code validates each claim, and only approved claims become sentences; that validator went through seven versions and catches 8 of 8 named defects. For archival images I added an evidence gate that makes the model say where in the frame it sees something, which fixed a false swastika report on a 1920s football-crowd photograph.

iv-cost.answer: I count cost per successful result rather than per call, and I set budgets before spending. In my Skyrule generation screen, a personal project, the better configuration used about a quarter of the output tokens per accepted group, and about half the model calls. Hosted spend has hard caps: the second-model review ledger is capped at $30, and image jobs for my picture books, also a personal project, carried a per-job dollar cap and used the Batch API at half price, 170 pictures for about $3.54. On-prem, the cheapest lever was the serving stack: continuous batching cut a 22-hour job to 3.7 hours on the same GPU. For procurement I estimated about $77 a month on Azure with gpt-4o-mini, and response caching by prompt hash makes repeat queries free.
